questiontext.text: The Metaheuristic Comparison explorer runs three search strategies on the same example. What does it compare them on?

answer.text: How quickly each strategy drives the best cost toward zero (coverage) — a convergence-and-coverage comparison of random search, hill climbing, and a genetic algorithm

feedback.text: Correct — the explorer runs all three side by side and charts best cost versus number of evaluations.

answer.text: Which strategy has the shortest source code

feedback.text: The explorer compares search behaviour (convergence and coverage), not code length.

answer.text: Which programming language runs the target function fastest

feedback.text: All strategies run on the same instrumented example; language speed is not what is compared.

answer.text: How many lines of the target function each strategy rewrites

feedback.text: The strategies generate test inputs; they never rewrite the target function.

generalfeedback.text: The comparison tab runs randomSearch, hillClimb, and geneticAlgorithm on one selected example (nested guard, triangle, or multimodal) and shows each strategy's coverage status, best cost, and a convergence chart of best cost against evaluations.

questiontext.text: In this explorer, what is random search?

answer.text: It samples input vectors uniformly at random and simply keeps the best (lowest-cost) one seen so far

feedback.text: Correct — random search draws inputs uniformly and remembers the best, with no guidance from cost.

answer.text: It moves from a start point to the best improving neighbour step by step

feedback.text: That is hill climbing, not random search.

answer.text: It evolves a population with crossover and mutation

feedback.text: That is the genetic algorithm, not random search.

answer.text: It enumerates every possible input in order

feedback.text: Random search samples at random; it does not exhaustively enumerate inputs.

generalfeedback.text: Random search is the unguided baseline: it repeatedly draws a random input vector, evaluates its cost, and keeps the lowest-cost individual found. It uses the cost only to decide which sample to remember, never to steer the next sample.

questiontext.text: In this explorer, what is hill climbing?

answer.text: From one random starting point it repeatedly moves to the best improving neighbour, stopping when no neighbour improves the cost

feedback.text: Correct — hill climbing is a single-trajectory local search that halts at a local optimum.

answer.text: It keeps a whole population of individuals and recombines them

feedback.text: That describes the genetic algorithm; hill climbing follows one trajectory.

answer.text: It draws every candidate uniformly at random

feedback.text: That is random search; hill climbing moves deliberately to improving neighbours.

answer.text: It always finds the global optimum given enough steps

feedback.text: Hill climbing can halt at a local optimum and never reach the global one.

generalfeedback.text: Hill climbing starts from a single random individual and, each step, examines the plus/minus-one neighbours, moving to the best one that lowers the cost. When no neighbour improves, it stops — it has reached a local optimum.

questiontext.text: In this explorer, what is a genetic algorithm (GA)?

answer.text: A population-based search that evolves many candidate inputs using selection, crossover, mutation, and elitism

feedback.text: Correct — the GA maintains a population and evolves it with these genetic operators.

answer.text: A single-trajectory search that moves to the best neighbour each step

feedback.text: That is hill climbing; the GA works on a whole population.

answer.text: Uniform random sampling with no operators

feedback.text: That is random search; the GA applies selection, crossover, and mutation.

answer.text: An exhaustive enumeration of the input space

feedback.text: The GA samples and evolves candidates; it does not enumerate the whole space.

generalfeedback.text: The genetic algorithm keeps a population (here 20 individuals), selects parents by tournament, forms offspring by one-point crossover, perturbs them by mutation, and carries the best individual forward unchanged (elitism), generation after generation.

questiontext.text: What is a local optimum in this search setting?

answer.text: A point whose neighbours are all at least as costly, so a local move cannot improve it, even though it may not cover the target

feedback.text: Correct — no neighbouring step lowers the cost, yet the global goal (cost 0) may be unreached.

answer.text: The input with the globally lowest possible cost, always cost 0

feedback.text: That is the global optimum; a local optimum need not reach cost 0.

answer.text: Any input drawn at random during the search

feedback.text: A random draw is not necessarily a local optimum.

answer.text: The starting point of a hill-climb run

feedback.text: The start is just an initial guess; a local optimum is where local moves stop improving.

generalfeedback.text: A local optimum is a solution that no small (neighbour) move can improve. Hill climbing halts there. It may still have positive cost — meaning the target branch is not covered — which is exactly the trap the explorer illustrates on the multimodal example.

questiontext.text: What is a population in the genetic algorithm?

answer.text: The set of candidate input vectors the GA maintains and evolves together each generation

feedback.text: Correct — the population is the collection of individuals evolved in parallel.

answer.text: The single current point of a hill-climb run

feedback.text: Hill climbing tracks one point; a population is many individuals at once.

answer.text: The total number of evaluations the budget allows

feedback.text: That is the evaluation budget, not the population.

answer.text: The list of branches in the target function

feedback.text: Branches belong to the program; the population is the GA's set of candidate inputs.

generalfeedback.text: A population is the group of candidate solutions (input vectors) the GA holds at once — here 20. Evolving a whole population, rather than a single point, is what lets the GA explore several regions of the search space simultaneously.

questiontext.text: Which strategy explores from a single starting point, moving to an improving neighbour each step?

answer.text: Hill climbing

feedback.text: Correct — hill climbing follows one trajectory from a single random start.

answer.text: Genetic algorithm

feedback.text: The GA evolves a whole population, not a single point.

answer.text: Random search

feedback.text: Random search draws independent samples; it does not follow a trajectory of neighbours.

answer.text: All three equally

feedback.text: Only hill climbing follows a single improving trajectory.

generalfeedback.text: Hill climbing is the one strategy defined by a single trajectory: one random start, then step-by-step moves to the best improving neighbour. Random search draws independent samples and the GA evolves a population.

questiontext.text: Which strategy maintains a population evolved with crossover and mutation?

answer.text: Genetic algorithm

feedback.text: Correct — only the GA keeps a population and applies crossover and mutation.

answer.text: Hill climbing

feedback.text: Hill climbing has one current point and no crossover or mutation.

answer.text: Random search

feedback.text: Random search draws independent uniform samples; it has no population or operators.

answer.text: None of them

feedback.text: The genetic algorithm is exactly the population-based strategy here.

generalfeedback.text: Crossover and mutation are genetic operators applied to a population. Only the genetic algorithm uses them; hill climbing and random search operate without a population.

questiontext.text: Which strategy samples inputs uniformly at random with no guidance from the cost when choosing the next input?

answer.text: Random search

feedback.text: Correct — random search draws each new input uniformly, ignoring cost when choosing it.

answer.text: Hill climbing

feedback.text: Hill climbing uses cost to pick the best improving neighbour; it is guided.

answer.text: Genetic algorithm

feedback.text: The GA uses cost for selection; its search is guided.

answer.text: All three

feedback.text: Only random search is unguided when choosing the next input.

generalfeedback.text: Random search is the unguided baseline: each new input is drawn uniformly at random, and cost is used only to decide which sample to keep. Hill climbing and the GA both use cost to steer the search.

questiontext.text: The explorer shows a Stuck badge on the hill-climbing panel. What does it indicate?

answer.text: Hill climbing stopped at a local optimum with positive best cost — no neighbour improved, and the target was not covered

feedback.text: Correct — the badge marks a run that halted at a local optimum without reaching cost 0.

answer.text: Hill climbing covered the target and stopped early

feedback.text: Covering the target means cost 0; the Stuck badge marks the opposite — a run that could not improve further.

answer.text: The chart failed to render

feedback.text: The badge is about the search outcome, not a rendering error.

answer.text: The genetic algorithm ran out of budget

feedback.text: The Stuck badge is shown only for hill climbing, not for the GA.

generalfeedback.text: The Stuck badge appears when the hill-climb result has positive best cost at termination — it moved to a local optimum where no neighbouring step lowered the cost, so the target branch was never covered.

questiontext.text: What does the explorer's convergence chart plot for each strategy?

answer.text: Best cost so far against the number of evaluations

feedback.text: Correct — each polyline traces best cost as evaluations accumulate.

answer.text: Source-code length against runtime

feedback.text: The chart tracks search progress (best cost vs evaluations), not code metrics.

answer.text: The population size against the generation number

feedback.text: Population size is fixed; the chart plots best cost over evaluations.

answer.text: The number of branches against the input value

feedback.text: The chart is about cost convergence, not branch counts.

generalfeedback.text: The convergence chart draws one polyline per strategy — best cost on the vertical axis, evaluation index on the horizontal axis — so you can see how fast each strategy drives cost down and whether it reaches zero.

name.text: What a lower best cost means

questiontext.text: In the explorer, a lower best cost means what, and what does a best cost of exactly 0 mean?

answer.text: Lower cost means closer to covering the target branch; a cost of 0 means the target is covered

feedback.text: Correct — cost measures distance to coverage, and cost 0 is exactly coverage.

answer.text: Lower cost means the code ran faster; 0 means instant

feedback.text: Cost measures distance to coverage, not runtime.

answer.text: Lower cost means fewer evaluations were used; 0 means none

feedback.text: Cost is about coverage distance, not the number of evaluations.

answer.text: Higher cost is better; 0 is the worst

feedback.text: It is the reverse — cost 0 is the goal, and lower is better.

generalfeedback.text: Cost is approach level plus normalized branch distance; it is zero exactly when the input covers the target branch. So driving best cost to 0 is the whole objective, and a strategy whose curve reaches 0 has achieved coverage.

questiontext.text: Hill climbing, as used in this explorer, maintains a whole population of candidate solutions each step.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — hill climbing tracks a single current point; only the genetic algorithm keeps a population.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — hill climbing follows one trajectory from one point; the population belongs to the GA.

generalfeedback.text: Hill climbing is a single-trajectory local search: it holds one current individual and moves to an improving neighbour. Maintaining a population of candidates evolved together is the defining feature of the genetic algorithm, not hill climbing.

questiontext.text: What is crossover in the genetic algorithm?

answer.text: An operator that combines parts of two parent individuals to form an offspring

feedback.text: Correct — crossover recombines two parents into a child.

answer.text: A random perturbation applied to a single individual's components

feedback.text: That is mutation, not crossover.

answer.text: Carrying the best individual unchanged to the next generation

feedback.text: That is elitism, not crossover.

answer.text: Drawing a brand-new individual uniformly at random

feedback.text: That is random initialization, not crossover.

generalfeedback.text: Crossover takes two selected parents and combines their components (here by a one-point cut) to build an offspring, letting good pieces from different parents come together. It is distinct from mutation (random perturbation) and elitism (carrying the best forward).

questiontext.text: What is mutation in the genetic algorithm?

answer.text: A small random change applied to an individual's components, introducing new variation

feedback.text: Correct — mutation randomly perturbs an individual to add diversity.

answer.text: Combining two parents into a child

feedback.text: That is crossover, not mutation.

answer.text: Selecting the fitter of two random individuals

feedback.text: That is tournament selection, not mutation.

answer.text: Moving to the best improving neighbour

feedback.text: That is a hill-climb step, not a GA mutation.

generalfeedback.text: Mutation perturbs an individual's components by small random amounts (with some per-component probability), injecting fresh variation into the population. This diversity is a key way the GA reaches regions that selection and crossover alone might not explore.

name.text: Why hill climbing loses to the GA on multimodal

questiontext.text: On the multimodal example, why does hill climbing underperform the genetic algorithm?

answer.text: A single hill-climb trajectory gets trapped in a local optimum that does not cover the target, while the GA population escapes such traps through diversity and its operators

feedback.text: Correct — this is exactly the local-optimum trap the explorer demonstrates.

answer.text: Hill climbing is given a smaller evaluation budget than the GA

feedback.text: Both run under the same budget; the difference is the local-optimum trap, not the budget.

answer.text: Hill climbing samples inputs uniformly at random, unlike the structured GA

feedback.text: Hill climbing is guided, not random; random sampling describes the baseline strategy.

answer.text: Hill climbing follows the gradient too aggressively and overshoots the optimum

feedback.text: The problem is being trapped at a local optimum, not overshooting a global one.

generalfeedback.text: The multimodal landscape has many basins. A single hill-climb run descends into one basin and halts at a local optimum with positive cost, missing the target. The GA's population and mutation keep enough diversity to escape those basins and reach coverage.

name.text: Why the modulo makes multimodal hard

questiontext.text: The multimodal example computes r = x % 20 and targets r == 7 and then x > 50. Why does this defeat hill climbing?

answer.text: The modulo makes the branch-distance landscape non-monotone, creating many basins; small plus/minus-one steps lead into a local optimum rather than toward the covering input

feedback.text: Correct — the non-monotone modulo landscape traps a local, step-by-step search.

answer.text: The modulo makes every input have the same cost, so no move ever improves

feedback.text: Costs do vary; the problem is that the landscape is non-monotone, not flat.

answer.text: The target branch is unreachable for every input

feedback.text: It is reachable — inputs such as 67 and 87 cover it; the issue is that local search cannot get there.

answer.text: Hill climbing cannot compute the modulo operator

feedback.text: The search only reads costs from the trace; it does not need to compute the modulo itself.

generalfeedback.text: Because x % 20 is non-monotone in x, the branch distance for r == 7 rises and falls repeatedly, carving many basins. A plus/minus-one search settles into one basin whose bottom does not satisfy both r == 7 and x > 50, so it gets stuck.

name.text: What a population adds over one trajectory

questiontext.text: What does maintaining a population add over a single hill-climb trajectory?

answer.text: It explores several regions of the search space at once, so the whole search is not doomed when one region is a dead-end local optimum

feedback.text: Correct — many individuals cover many basins, giving the search a way out of any single trap.

answer.text: It guarantees the global optimum is found in one generation

feedback.text: A population improves the odds of escaping traps but guarantees nothing in a single generation.

answer.text: It removes the need to evaluate cost at all

feedback.text: The GA still evaluates cost for every individual; the population is about coverage of the space.

answer.text: It makes each evaluation cheaper

feedback.text: Per-evaluation cost is unchanged; the benefit is exploring multiple regions simultaneously.

generalfeedback.text: A single trajectory can only ever be in one place, so one bad basin dooms it. A population spreads individuals across many basins; selection concentrates effort on the promising ones while others keep exploring, which is how the GA avoids the trap that stops hill climbing.

questiontext.text: What does mutation contribute to the genetic algorithm's search?

answer.text: It injects fresh random variation, letting the population reach inputs that selection and crossover alone would not produce — helping it escape local optima

feedback.text: Correct — mutation is the diversity source that keeps the search from stagnating.

answer.text: It carries the best individual unchanged to the next generation

feedback.text: That is elitism, not mutation.

answer.text: It guarantees every offspring has lower cost than its parents

feedback.text: Mutation is random; it can raise or lower cost, and offers no such guarantee.

answer.text: It sorts the population by cost

feedback.text: Sorting/ranking relates to selection, not mutation.

generalfeedback.text: Mutation randomly perturbs components of an individual, adding variation the current population lacks. Without it, selection and crossover could converge prematurely; with it, the population keeps reaching new regions, which is central to escaping local optima.

questiontext.text: What does crossover contribute in a multi-variable example such as the triangle classifier (inputs a, b, c)?

answer.text: It recombines components from two parents, so a child can inherit good values on some variables from one parent and on others from the second

feedback.text: Correct — crossover mixes partial solutions across variables from different parents.

answer.text: It applies a random perturbation to a single individual

feedback.text: That is mutation, not crossover.

answer.text: It discards the whole population and restarts randomly

feedback.text: Crossover builds offspring from parents; it does not restart the search.

answer.text: It measures how many branches were covered

feedback.text: Crossover is a reproduction operator, not a coverage measurement.

generalfeedback.text: With several input variables, one parent may already have a good value for a and another a good value for c. A one-point crossover can combine those into a single child, assembling partial solutions faster than mutation alone.

questiontext.text: On the multimodal example, what does the explorer typically show on the hill-climbing panel?

answer.text: A Stuck badge, a not-covered / budget-exhausted status, and a best cost above zero

feedback.text: Correct — the seed is chosen so hill climbing halts at a local optimum without covering the target.

answer.text: Covered, with a best cost of exactly zero

feedback.text: Hill climbing does not cover the multimodal target; that is the point of the example.

answer.text: An empty panel with no result

feedback.text: The panel shows a completed (stuck) run, not an empty result.

answer.text: A Stuck badge but a best cost of zero

feedback.text: If the best cost were zero the target would be covered, which contradicts being stuck.

generalfeedback.text: For the multimodal example the explorer deliberately picks a hill-climb seed that lands in a local optimum without covering the target, so the panel carries the Stuck badge, reports budget exhausted / not covered, and shows a best cost strictly above zero.

questiontext.text: On the multimodal example, what does the explorer show for the genetic algorithm, according to the takeaway?

answer.text: It covers the target — the GA consistently finds coverage goals that hill climbing misses on multimodal landscapes

feedback.text: Correct — that is precisely the explorer's stated takeaway.

answer.text: It also gets stuck at the same local optimum as hill climbing

feedback.text: The takeaway is that the GA finds goals hill climbing misses, so it does not share the trap.

answer.text: It never finishes within the budget

feedback.text: The GA reaches coverage on this example; it does not merely exhaust the budget.

answer.text: It refuses to run without crossover

feedback.text: The GA runs on this single-variable example; the takeaway is that it covers the target.

generalfeedback.text: The explorer's takeaway states that genetic algorithms consistently find coverage goals that hill climbing misses on multimodal landscapes — so the GA panel reports coverage where the hill-climbing panel is stuck.

name.text: Match: which is guided local search

questiontext.text: Which strategy is best described as guided local search — using cost to move, but confined to one region?

answer.text: Hill climbing

feedback.text: Correct — it uses cost to pick the best neighbour but stays within one basin, a local search.

answer.text: Random search

feedback.text: Random search is unguided global sampling, not guided local search.

answer.text: Genetic algorithm

feedback.text: The GA is a guided but population-based global search, not confined to one region.

answer.text: None of them use cost

feedback.text: Both hill climbing and the GA use cost; hill climbing is the local one.

generalfeedback.text: Hill climbing is guided (it follows cost to the best neighbour) yet local (it stays in the region of its start). Random search is unguided global sampling; the GA is guided global search over a population.

name.text: Why include random search as a baseline

questiontext.text: Why is random search included in the comparison at all?

answer.text: As an unguided baseline: it shows what search guidance actually buys, since a guided strategy that cannot beat random search offers no real advantage

feedback.text: Correct — random search is the reference point that guidance must improve upon.

answer.text: Because it is guaranteed to be the fastest on every example

feedback.text: Random search is unguided and often not the fastest; it is a baseline, not a champion.

answer.text: Because it always fails, making the others look good

feedback.text: Random search can succeed (e.g. when covering inputs are plentiful); it is an honest baseline, not a strawman.

answer.text: Because it is the only strategy that uses the cost function

feedback.text: It is the one strategy that does not use cost to steer; hill climbing and the GA do.

generalfeedback.text: A baseline sets the bar. Random search makes no use of cost to steer, so it shows how hard coverage is by luck alone. Guided strategies earn their complexity only by beating this baseline; on easy examples random search may already suffice.

name.text: Reading a curve that reaches zero

questiontext.text: In the convergence chart, a strategy's curve reaches the bottom (cost 0) while another's flattens above it. What does that show?

answer.text: The curve reaching 0 achieved coverage; the one flattening above 0 stalled without covering the target

feedback.text: Correct — cost 0 is coverage, and a flat positive plateau is a stalled (e.g. stuck) search.

answer.text: Both strategies covered the target; the heights are arbitrary

feedback.text: Only the curve at 0 covered the target; a positive plateau means no coverage.

answer.text: The higher curve is better because it used fewer evaluations

feedback.text: Lower cost is better; a higher plateau means the target was not reached.

answer.text: The flattening curve will always drop to 0 with a few more evaluations

feedback.text: A plateau at a local optimum can persist regardless of extra evaluations.

generalfeedback.text: The vertical axis is best cost, so a curve reaching 0 has covered the target, and a curve that flattens at a positive value has stalled — typically hill climbing stuck at a local optimum, while the GA's curve descends all the way to 0.

name.text: Why a special hill-climb seed is chosen

questiontext.text: For the multimodal example the explorer scans several seeds for the hill-climb run. Why?

answer.text: To reliably pick a start that lands in a local optimum without covering the target, so the panel clearly illustrates the trap

feedback.text: Correct — the scan finds a seed where hill climbing is stuck and not covered, making the lesson visible.

answer.text: To find the seed that lets hill climbing cover the target fastest

feedback.text: It is the opposite — the scan looks for a seed where hill climbing gets stuck without covering.

answer.text: To give hill climbing a larger evaluation budget than the others

feedback.text: The budget is unchanged; only the starting seed is chosen.

answer.text: To randomise the GA's population

feedback.text: The seed scan concerns the hill-climb start, not the GA population.

generalfeedback.text: On the multimodal example the explorer scans seeds and picks one where the hill-climb run ends stuck and uncovered. This makes the local-optimum trap reproducible and clearly visible next to the GA, which does reach coverage.

questiontext.text: When hill climbing chooses its next move, what information guides it?

answer.text: The cost of each neighbour — it moves to the neighbour with the lowest cost, provided that cost is an improvement

feedback.text: Correct — hill climbing is greedy on the fitness/cost of neighbouring inputs.

answer.text: A coin flip — it picks a neighbour uniformly at random

feedback.text: That would be a random walk; hill climbing chooses the best improving neighbour by cost.

answer.text: The generation number of the GA

feedback.text: Hill climbing is independent of the GA's generations.

answer.text: The order in which branches appear in the source

feedback.text: It is guided by neighbour cost, not by source ordering.

generalfeedback.text: Each step, hill climbing evaluates the plus/minus-one neighbours and moves to the one with the lowest cost, as long as that lowers the current cost. The cost — approach level plus normalized branch distance — is the gradient signal it follows.

questiontext.text: The genetic algorithm uses elitism. What does that guarantee about the best cost across generations?

answer.text: The best individual is carried forward unchanged, so the best cost never gets worse from one generation to the next

feedback.text: Correct — elitism makes the best cost monotonically non-increasing.

answer.text: Every individual in the next generation is at least as good as every individual in the current one

feedback.text: Elitism protects only the single best individual, not every member of the population.

answer.text: The population size shrinks each generation

feedback.text: Population size is fixed; elitism concerns which individual is preserved, not the size.

answer.text: Mutation is disabled for the elite's offspring

feedback.text: Elitism preserves the elite itself; it does not disable mutation elsewhere.

generalfeedback.text: Elitism carries the best-so-far individual into the next generation untouched. Because that individual (and thus its cost) survives, the best cost can only stay the same or improve — it never regresses, which is why the GA's convergence curve is monotonically non-increasing.

name.text: Why hill climbing succeeds on nested guard

questiontext.text: Hill climbing covers the nested-guard example (x == 17 then y > 100) but not multimodal. Why the difference?

answer.text: The nested-guard branch distances vary smoothly and monotonically toward the target, so local plus/minus-one steps descend to coverage, whereas the modulo makes multimodal non-monotone

feedback.text: Correct — a smooth landscape rewards local search; a non-monotone one traps it.

answer.text: The nested-guard example has no branches to cover

feedback.text: It has a nested target branch; the point is that its landscape is smooth.

answer.text: Hill climbing is given more evaluations on nested guard

feedback.text: The budget is the same; the difference is the shape of the landscape.

answer.text: The GA cannot run on the nested-guard example

feedback.text: All three strategies run on every example; the question is why hill climbing succeeds here.

generalfeedback.text: For x == 17 and y > 100, branch distance decreases steadily as x nears 17 and y nears 100, so plus/minus-one steps climb straight to coverage. The multimodal modulo instead makes the landscape rise and fall, so local steps stall in a basin.

name.text: Population plus mutation can escape a trap

questiontext.text: A genetic algorithm can escape a local optimum that traps a single hill-climb run, because its population and mutation maintain diversity across the search space.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — population diversity and mutation let the GA reach basins a single trajectory cannot.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The GA's population and mutation are exactly what let it escape traps that stop a single hill-climb trajectory.

generalfeedback.text: A single hill-climb trajectory is confined to one basin and halts at its local optimum. The GA keeps many individuals spread across the space and adds random mutation, so even if some individuals sit in a bad basin, others (or their mutated offspring) can reach the covering region.

questiontext.text: On multimodal, hill climbing reaches an input where x % 20 == 7 but x <= 50 (for example x = 47, so the first guard is satisfied but x > 50 is not). Why can it not improve from here?

answer.text: Raising x by one breaks x % 20 == 7, which fails the outer guard and raises the approach level, so cost goes up; the covering inputs (67, 87) are many steps away and unreachable by single improving moves

feedback.text: Correct — either neighbour raises cost, so it is a local optimum that never covers the target.

answer.text: Both neighbours lower the cost, so it keeps moving and eventually covers

feedback.text: If a neighbour lowered cost it would not be stuck; here both neighbours raise it.

answer.text: The cost is already zero, so there is nothing to improve

feedback.text: The target x > 50 is unmet, so cost is positive, not zero.

answer.text: The evaluation budget is exhausted at exactly this point

feedback.text: The trap is structural: it halts because no neighbour improves, independent of the budget.

generalfeedback.text: At x = 47 the outer guard x % 20 == 7 holds but x > 50 does not, so cost is the normalized distance for that comparison. Stepping to x = 46 or x = 48 makes x % 20 leave 7, which fails the first guard and adds a whole approach level — a higher cost. Both neighbours are worse, so hill climbing stops, and the nearest covering inputs (67, 87) are unreachable by single improving steps.

questiontext.text: In terms of exploration versus exploitation, how do hill climbing and the GA differ, and what does hill climbing's stance cost it?

answer.text: Hill climbing is almost pure exploitation of the local gradient, so it converges fast but can be trapped; the GA balances exploitation (selection) with exploration (population diversity and mutation), trading some speed for the ability to escape traps

feedback.text: Correct — that trade-off is exactly why the GA reaches coverage the local search misses.

answer.text: Both are pure exploration, so neither can converge

feedback.text: Hill climbing exploits the gradient greedily; it is not pure exploration.

answer.text: Hill climbing explores globally while the GA only exploits

feedback.text: It is the reverse: hill climbing is local exploitation; the GA adds global exploration.

answer.text: Exploration and exploitation are irrelevant to search-based testing

feedback.text: They are the central trade-off distinguishing these strategies.

generalfeedback.text: Hill climbing exploits: it greedily follows the local gradient and converges quickly, but pure exploitation gets stuck at the first local optimum. The GA mixes exploitation (fitness-based selection and elitism) with exploration (population diversity and mutation), which is slower per unit of progress but escapes basins that trap a purely local search.

questiontext.text: On which kind of landscape does the GA's advantage over hill climbing disappear?

answer.text: On a smooth, essentially unimodal landscape (like the nested guard), where local search already descends straight to coverage, so the GA's extra machinery buys nothing and may even be slower

feedback.text: Correct — when there is no local-optimum trap, the simpler local search suffices.

answer.text: On a landscape with many deceptive local optima

feedback.text: That is where the GA's advantage is largest, not where it disappears.

answer.text: On any landscape, because the GA is always strictly better

feedback.text: The GA is not universally better; on smooth landscapes hill climbing matches it more cheaply.

answer.text: Whenever the evaluation budget is large

feedback.text: Budget size is not what removes the GA's edge; landscape shape is.

generalfeedback.text: The GA earns its keep only when there are traps to escape. On a smooth, unimodal landscape such as the nested guard, hill climbing walks straight down to cost 0, and the GA's population, crossover, and mutation add overhead without adding value. There is no free lunch: the best strategy depends on the landscape.

name.text: Crossover is not the source of the edge on multimodal

questiontext.text: The multimodal example has a single input variable x. Given that, why is crossover not the source of the GA's advantage here?

answer.text: With one variable, one-point crossover has nothing to recombine and effectively returns a parent copy, so the GA's edge on multimodal comes from population diversity and mutation, not crossover

feedback.text: Correct — single-variable crossover is a no-op, so diversity and mutation do the work.

answer.text: Crossover mixes the x values of two parents to produce an intermediate x, which is what covers the target

feedback.text: One-point crossover on a single component cannot produce an intermediate value; it just copies a parent.

answer.text: Crossover is disabled for all examples in the explorer

feedback.text: Crossover runs; it is simply a no-op when there is only one variable to cut.

answer.text: Crossover is the only operator that matters, even with one variable

feedback.text: With one variable there is no cut point, so crossover contributes nothing here.

generalfeedback.text: One-point crossover needs at least two components to have a meaningful cut. The multimodal example has a single variable, so crossover returns a copy of a parent and contributes nothing. The GA still beats hill climbing here purely through its population diversity and mutation — a good reminder to attribute each strategy's properties precisely.

questiontext.text: On multimodal, the hill-climb curve drops below the random curve early but then flattens above zero, while the GA curve descends more gradually and reaches zero. What does this pattern illustrate?

answer.text: Hill climbing converges quickly on its local gradient but gets trapped, while the GA makes slower, broader progress that ultimately achieves coverage — fast-but-local versus slower-but-global

feedback.text: Correct — the shapes capture the exploitation-versus-exploration trade-off directly.

answer.text: Random search is the best strategy because its curve starts highest

feedback.text: Starting high is not an advantage; the GA is the one that reaches coverage.

answer.text: The GA is worse because it takes more evaluations to start improving

feedback.text: Reaching cost 0 is the goal; the GA's broader search is what gets there.

answer.text: Hill climbing will reach zero if you read the chart long enough

feedback.text: Its curve flattens at a local optimum; it will not reach zero however long you look.

generalfeedback.text: The early steep drop of the hill-climb curve is fast local exploitation; its flat positive tail is the local-optimum trap. The GA's more gradual descent to zero reflects a broader, population-driven search that pays a little early speed to gain global reach and coverage.

name.text: Random restarts and the population analogy

questiontext.text: A single hill-climb run has no restarts. How would adding random restarts relate to the GA's population?

answer.text: Random restarts run several independent hill climbs from different starts, giving multiple chances to find a good basin — similar in spirit to how the GA's population spreads across many basins at once

feedback.text: Correct — restarts approximate parallel local searches, echoing the population's coverage of the space.

answer.text: Random restarts guarantee the global optimum in a single run

feedback.text: Restarts improve the odds but guarantee nothing.

answer.text: Random restarts would make hill climbing identical to random search

feedback.text: Between restarts it still climbs the gradient locally; it is not pure random sampling.

answer.text: Random restarts remove the need to evaluate cost

feedback.text: Each restarted climb still evaluates cost to choose neighbours.

generalfeedback.text: Restarting hill climbing from several random starts explores several basins, much as the GA's population occupies several basins simultaneously. The population can additionally share information via selection and crossover, but the core intuition — many starts beat one when the landscape has traps — is shared.

name.text: Unlimited budget does not save hill climbing

questiontext.text: Suppose you gave hill climbing an unlimited evaluation budget on the multimodal example. Would it then cover the target?

answer.text: No — it terminates as soon as no neighbour improves the cost, so once it reaches a local optimum extra budget changes nothing

feedback.text: Correct — the halt is structural (a local optimum), not caused by running out of budget.

answer.text: Yes — with enough evaluations any local search reaches the global optimum

feedback.text: A basic hill climb stops at a local optimum regardless of remaining budget.

answer.text: Yes — the extra budget lets it try new random starts automatically

feedback.text: This hill climb has no restarts; it just stops when no neighbour improves.

answer.text: Only if the population size is increased

feedback.text: Hill climbing has no population; the issue is that it halts at a local optimum.

generalfeedback.text: Plain hill climbing stops the moment no neighbouring step lowers the cost. At a local optimum that condition holds forever, so no amount of extra budget helps. Escaping requires a different mechanism — random restarts, or a population as in the GA.

name.text: Why approach level dominates branch distance

questiontext.text: The cost is approach level plus a normalized branch distance in the range [0, 1). Why does the approach level dominate the total cost?

answer.text: Approach level is a whole number of unsatisfied nesting levels, while normalized branch distance is always below 1, so being one nesting level further from the target always costs more than any branch distance within a level

feedback.text: Correct — the integer approach level outweighs the sub-1 branch-distance term.

answer.text: Branch distance is always larger than the approach level

feedback.text: Normalized branch distance is below 1, so it cannot exceed a whole approach level.

answer.text: Approach level is normalized to [0, 1) and branch distance is an integer

feedback.text: It is the other way round: approach level is the integer, branch distance is normalized below 1.

answer.text: The two terms are added only when the target is already covered

feedback.text: They are combined precisely when the target is not yet covered; once covered the cost is 0.

generalfeedback.text: Approach level counts how many enclosing guards are still unsatisfied — an integer — while branch distance is squashed into [0, 1). So reducing the approach level (getting past an outer guard) always lowers cost more than any improvement in branch distance at the current level, which is why the search first tries to enter deeper nesting before fine-tuning the final comparison.

name.text: Why the GA curve never rises

questiontext.text: Why does the genetic algorithm's best-cost curve never rise across generations in the explorer?

answer.text: Best cost tracks the lowest cost seen so far and elitism preserves the best individual, so the recorded best can only stay level or fall

feedback.text: Correct — a running minimum protected by elitism is monotonically non-increasing.

answer.text: Because mutation can only ever decrease an individual's cost

feedback.text: Mutation is random and can raise cost; monotonicity comes from tracking the best-so-far, not from mutation.

answer.text: Because the GA re-sorts the whole population every evaluation

feedback.text: Sorting does not explain a monotone best-cost curve; tracking a running minimum does.

answer.text: Because the population size grows each generation

feedback.text: Population size is fixed; the curve is monotone because it records the best-so-far.

generalfeedback.text: The plotted value is the best cost found up to that evaluation — a running minimum. Individual offspring can be worse than their parents, but the recorded best only updates when something better appears, and elitism keeps the current best alive, so the curve is monotonically non-increasing.

name.text: Why random search still covers multimodal

questiontext.text: Random search has no guidance, yet it can still cover the multimodal target, whose inputs range over x in [0, 100] with only x = 67 and x = 87 covering. Why here, and why is this not a general endorsement of random search?

answer.text: The space is tiny (about 101 values) with a generous budget, so uniform sampling almost certainly hits a covering value; in larger or sparser spaces the odds collapse and unguided sampling scales badly

feedback.text: Correct — luck works when covering inputs are relatively common and the budget dwarfs the space, but not in general.

answer.text: Random search is guided toward covering values, so it reliably finds them

feedback.text: Random search is unguided; it succeeds here by sheer sampling density, not guidance.

answer.text: Random search always covers any target given enough time, so it is generally the best strategy

feedback.text: In vast or sparse spaces the required samples explode; coverage by luck does not scale.

answer.text: The multimodal target is actually unreachable, so no strategy covers it

feedback.text: It is reachable at x = 67 and x = 87; random search hits one of these by chance.

generalfeedback.text: With roughly 101 possible x values and a budget far larger than that, uniform random sampling is nearly certain to draw a covering value (67 or 87). But this is a property of a tiny, dense target space; in realistic programs the covering region is a vanishing fraction of an enormous space, so unguided sampling becomes hopeless and guidance is what pays off.

name.text: Population size trade-off under a fixed budget

questiontext.text: Under a fixed evaluation budget, what is the tension in choosing the GA's population size?

answer.text: A larger population explores more per generation but, since each individual costs an evaluation, the budget allows fewer generations; too small under-explores and too large leaves too little evolution

feedback.text: Correct — population size and generation count trade off against each other under a fixed budget.

answer.text: There is no tension; larger populations are strictly better under any budget

feedback.text: A larger population consumes the budget faster, leaving fewer generations to evolve.

answer.text: Population size has no effect on how the budget is spent

feedback.text: Every individual is an evaluation, so population size directly determines how the budget is spent.

answer.text: A smaller population always converges to the global optimum faster

feedback.text: Too small a population under-explores and is more prone to premature convergence.

generalfeedback.text: Each individual evaluated spends part of the budget. A big population samples many regions per generation but burns the budget in few generations, limiting refinement; a tiny population evolves for many generations but explores too little and can converge prematurely. The right size balances breadth against the number of generations affordable.

questiontext.text: Why does the explorer let you compare the strategies across several examples rather than just one?

answer.text: Because a strategy's ranking depends on the landscape — the GA clearly wins only on the multimodal (trap-laden) example, so a single example could mislead about which strategy is best

feedback.text: Correct — comparing across landscapes shows that the best strategy is problem-dependent.

answer.text: Because more examples make the convergence chart look nicer

feedback.text: The reason is validity of the comparison, not aesthetics.

answer.text: Because each example uses a different cost function unrelated to the others

feedback.text: All examples use the same approach-level-plus-branch-distance cost; what differs is the landscape shape.

answer.text: Because the GA can only run on the triangle example

feedback.text: The GA runs on all examples; multiple examples reveal how ranking changes with the landscape.

generalfeedback.text: On smooth landscapes (nested guard) hill climbing is as good and cheaper; the GA's advantage shows up on the trap-laden multimodal example. Comparing across examples prevents the mistake of crowning one strategy from a single, unrepresentative landscape.

name.text: Why only hill climbing shows Stuck

questiontext.text: The Stuck badge appears only on the hill-climbing panel, never on random search or the GA. Why?

answer.text: Only hill climbing has a local-optimum termination condition (no improving neighbour) that leaves it stuck with positive cost; random search and the GA run until coverage or the budget ends, so no equivalent stuck state is reported

feedback.text: Correct — the stuck state is specific to a local search that halts when no neighbour improves.

answer.text: Random search and the GA always cover the target, so they can never be stuck

feedback.text: They can also fail to cover, but they simply exhaust the budget rather than halt at a local optimum.

answer.text: The badge is randomly assigned to one panel each run

feedback.text: The badge reflects the hill-climb result's stuck flag, not a random choice.

answer.text: The GA hides its stuck state to look better

feedback.text: The GA has no local-optimum halt to hide; it runs to coverage or budget.

generalfeedback.text: Being stuck means halting at a local optimum with cost still positive — a condition that only hill climbing's stop rule produces. Random search and the GA do not stop early on a local optimum; they either reach coverage or use up the budget, so there is no stuck state to badge.

name.text: Characterize each strategy's use of cost

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly characterizes how each strategy uses the cost (fitness) when deciding what to try next?

answer.text: Random search ignores cost when choosing the next input (using it only to keep the best); hill climbing greedily follows the local cost gradient; the GA uses cost for selection pressure while keeping diversity

feedback.text: Correct — none, greedy-local, and selection-guided-global respectively.

answer.text: All three ignore cost entirely and rely on luck

feedback.text: Hill climbing and the GA both use cost to steer; only random search ignores it when choosing.

answer.text: All three greedily follow the local gradient like hill climbing

feedback.text: Random search does not follow a gradient, and the GA balances selection with exploration.

answer.text: Random search follows the gradient while the GA and hill climbing sample uniformly

feedback.text: That inverts reality: random search is the uniform one; the others use cost to steer.

generalfeedback.text: The three sit on a spectrum of how much they exploit the fitness signal to choose the next input: random search not at all (it only keeps the best seen), hill climbing greedily and locally, and the GA through selection pressure that concentrates on fitter individuals while mutation and population diversity keep it exploring.

name.text: GA is not universally the best choice

questiontext.text: Because the GA covers the multimodal target where hill climbing gets stuck, the genetic algorithm is therefore the best choice for every coverage target.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — on smooth landscapes hill climbing reaches coverage just as well and more cheaply; the GA's advantage is landscape-dependent.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — there is no universally best strategy; the GA wins only where local optima trap simpler searches.

generalfeedback.text: The GA's win on multimodal comes from its ability to escape local optima, which matters only when such traps exist. On a smooth landscape like the nested guard, hill climbing covers the target with far less machinery. The right strategy depends on the problem's landscape — no single one dominates everywhere.
